title: Hashing.consistentHash() allocates a new object on every call
body:
### Guava Version

33.6.0-jre

### Description

I was building a load balancer that routes incoming requests to backend shards using consistent hashing. My hot path calls Hashing.consistentHash(hashCode, numBuckets) for every request — several thousand times per second under normal traffic.

While profiling with async-profiler, I noticed a steady stream of LinearCongruentialGenerator allocations showing up in the allocation flamegraph, all originating from consistentHash. I dug into the source and found that every single call to consistentHash allocates a new LinearCongruentialGenerator object. That class holds exactly one long field. There is no reason for it to be a heap-allocated object at all — the field and the arithmetic it performs could be local variables inside consistentHash itself.

Under heavy traffic this generates constant GC pressure for no gain. Inlining the single field and the formula from nextDouble() directly into consistentHash would make the allocation disappear entirely with zero behavioral change.

Relevant source: Hashing.java line 657, LinearCongruentialGenerator inner class lines 825–836.

How to reproduce:

Run the following code and attach an allocation profiler (e.g., async-profiler with -e alloc, or JVM flag -Xlog:gc to watch minor GC frequency):
HashCode hash = Hashing.murmur3_128().hashLong(42L);
for (int i = 0; i < 10_000_000; i++) {
    Hashing.consistentHash(hash, 100);
}
Observe LinearCongruentialGenerator objects appearing in the allocation profile at a rate of one per consistentHash call.
Alternatively, open Hashing.java and inspect line 657 — a new LinearCongruentialGenerator(input) allocation appears unconditionally on every call path.

### Example

```java
Example: Imagine a postal sorting facility that assigns each incoming letter to one of 100 bins using a fixed formula written on a reference card. For every single letter, instead of using the same card on the desk, a worker takes a blank sheet, hand-writes the formula on it, uses it once, and throws it away. The formula never changes — writing a new sheet for every letter is pure waste. The formula should just live on the desk as a few local variables, ready to use for the next letter the moment the current one is sorted.
```

### Expected Behavior

1. consistentHash computes and returns the correct bucket index using only stack-allocated local variables.
2. No heap objects are allocated per call beyond the method frame itself.
3. Under high call frequency the method contributes zero allocation pressure to the GC.

### Actual Behavior

1. A new LinearCongruentialGenerator instance is heap-allocated on every single call, regardless of call frequency.
2. Under high throughput (e.g., thousands of calls per second) this generates a continuous stream of short-lived objects, increasing minor GC frequency and adding measurable latency spikes in allocation-profiler traces.

### Packages

com.google.common.hash

### Platforms

_No response_

> There is no reason for it to be a heap-allocated object at all — the field and the arithmetic it performs could be local variables inside consistentHash itself.

We do use `LinearCongruentialGenerator` in exactly one other place internally, so not duplicating the arithmetic would be a reason. Maybe we should replace it with two static functions: `long nextState(long state)` and `double nextDouble(long state)`.

I’d like to work on this issue.

I explored the implementation and the allocation appears to come from the per-call `LinearCongruentialGenerator` instantiation inside `consistentHash()`.

My plan is to refactor the generator logic into allocation-free static helper methods (similar to the suggestion above), while preserving existing behavior and tests.

Please let me know if there are any constraints/preferences before I open a PR.

Hi [chaoren](https://github.com/chaoren), [abhinav-1504](https://github.com/abhinav-1504), 

Thanks for the context. I have started the implementation already as well and I'd like to share the approach I'm pursuing, which I believe goes further than introducing static helper methods as abinav has suggested.

My approach:

Rather than replacing LinearCongruentialGenerator with two static functions (nextState and nextDouble), the plan is to move the generator's single piece of mutable state - a long - directly into consistentHash() as a local variable, and run the two arithmetic steps inline on every loop iteration. The class itself is then deleted in full.

In plain terms: instead of creating a generator object that holds one number, you just keep that number in the method directly. There is no object, no constructor, no field read - just a local variable that gets updated each iteration the same way the class was updating its field.
I will be opening a PR soon if thats okay with the team. Thanks

We have one other user of this internally, so neither of you can work on it because you can't update that other caller.

We can inline just the `long state` and operate on it with the two static methods. The two methods would be small enough that they can be inlined by the JVM anyway, so there would be no difference in performance and it'll still allow us to reuse the same operations elsewhere.

Hi [chaoren](https://github.com/chaoren),

Thank you for the clarification on the internal caller - I was not aware it existed outside the public repo. That constraint is clear and I accept it: the class cannot be deleted.

To be transparent: I have already implemented and submitted a PR (#8426) based on full inlining. The PR eliminates the new LinearCongruentialGenerator(input) allocation in consistentHash by introducing a local long state variable and running the two arithmetic steps directly in the loop body. All 42 HashingTest cases pass and the full ./mvnw clean install completes with zero failures.

On the static helper approach - I want to be precise rather than dismissive. You are correct that the JVM will likely inline two small static methods in steady state, and I agree the practical difference at that point is negligible. The concern I would raise is that "likely inlined by the JVM" is a runtime assumption, not a compile-time guarantee. JIT inlining depends on bytecode size thresholds, code cache pressure, and call chain depth limits. Full inlining is fast by construction; the static method approach is fast by hope. In a hot path called thousands of times per second, that distinction is most visible during the warm-up window before JIT fires.

That said, I understand the constraint is real. I am happy to adapt the existing PR to your suggested approach - keeping the class for the internal caller, adding nextState(long) and nextDouble(long) as private static methods, and using a local long state in consistentHash to call them. The allocation is still eliminated, which is the core of the issue. Please let me know if you would like me to update the PR in that direction.
The two static methods are tiny. They are well within any reasonable size threshold for unconditional inlining. We also prefer code clarity over premature optimization.

title: forString() incorrectly parsing IPv4 mapped IPv6 address
body:
### Guava Version

33.1.2

### Description

When parsing an IPv4 mapped IPv6 address the InetAddresses.forString() incorrectly returns the address as a v4 address. 

### Example

```java
String ::ffff:10.111.184.37 -> Inet4Address "/10.111.184.37"
```

### Actual Behavior

I'm not sure who the best networking expert for me to ask about this is nowadays. Can you give me your analysis of the tradeoffs here? As a starting point, I asked Gemini, and I got the response below: ---

Here is a breakdown of the architectural and practical arguments for both approaches.

What is an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address?

Before weighing the arguments, it is helpful to visualize the structure. These addresses are defined in RFC 4291. They consist of 80 bits of zeros, 16 bits of ones, and then the 32 bits of the IPv4 address.

They are primarily used to allow IPv6 sockets to communicate with legacy IPv4 nodes.

Arguments for Returning an IPv6 Object

The "Purist" or "Structural" Approach.

Most standard libraries (like Python's ipaddress or Go's net package) often lean this way because, technically, the input is 128 bits long.

  • Data Fidelity (Losslessness): If the input string was ::ffff:192.0.2.1, returning an IPv4 object (192.0.2.1) discards information. You have technically altered the data type from what was provided. Returning an IPv6 object preserves the exact state of the input.

  • Socket API Consistency: In dual-stack socket programming, the operating system kernel often exposes these addresses as AF_INET6 (IPv6 family). If a library automatically converts them to IPv4, it creates a mismatch between the socket family and the address object, which can cause bugs in low-level networking code.

  • Avoids Ambiguity: If the library converts mapped addresses to IPv4, but not compatible addresses (::192.0.2.1, which is deprecated but exists), the behavior becomes unpredictable. Treating all 128-bit inputs as IPv6 is a simpler, more deterministic rule.

  • Security (Canonicalization): Automatic unmapping can be dangerous. If an Access Control List (ACL) blocks ::ffff:10.0.0.1 but allows 10.0.0.1, and your parser silently converts the former to the latter, you might accidentally bypass a security rule intended to block IPv6 traffic.

Arguments for Returning an IPv4 Object

The "Pragmatic" or "Semantic" Approach.

This approach argues that the identity of the host is what matters, not the container (the 128-bit format).

  • Usability & Developer Intent: When a developer parses ::ffff:192.168.1.1, they usually want to know "Which machine is this?" The answer is the IPv4 host 192.168.1.1. Requiring the developer to manually "unmap" the address every time is cumbersome.

  • Protocol Reality: An IPv4-mapped address is not valid for global IPv6 routing. It will never appear in an IPv6 packet header on the wire; it effectively is an IPv4 connection wrapped in an API abstraction. Treating it as IPv4 reflects the actual wire protocol being used.

  • Database Compatibility: If you are storing IP addresses in a database column typed for IPv4 (e.g., PostgreSQL inet or a VARCHAR(15)), returning an IPv6 object forces the user to add type-checking logic before saving, whereas an IPv4 object would "just work."

Comparison Summary

Feature | Return as IPv6 | Return as IPv4 -- | -- | -- Strictness | High (Structure focused) | Low (Utility focused) Information Loss | None | Loses the ::ffff: prefix Socket Matching | Matches AF_INET6 | Matches AF_INET Best For | Systems programming, Firewalls | Web apps, Analytics, Logging

The "Hybrid" Solution

Many modern libraries solve this by returning an IPv6 object but providing a helper method. For example:

  1. Return IPv6 by default: To maintain structural correctness.

  2. Provide properties: Such as .ipv4_mapped (boolean) or .teredo (boolean).

  3. Provide a method: Such as .map_to_ipv4() or .unwrap() which explicitly converts it to the IPv4 object if valid.

This forces the developer to be explicit about the conversion, mitigating security risks while acknowledging the utility of the underlying IPv4 address.

I dug up a comment in some long-deleted code that suggests that `InetAddress.getByAddress` might autoconvert. If that's the case, then that would be one argument in favor of making our method do the same.

The particular case where this was observed was when processing data acquired from network devices where some vendors expose an IPv6 address using this notation. It's problematic because it is a valid IPv6 address, as reported by the device, but the current net library's behavior makes it effectively a v4 address and checks for isIpv6 fail.

Canonically, an address like ::ffff:a.b.c.d is an IPv6 address type, not IPv4. What it gets used for is a different matter.

It seems pretty clear to me that the behavior is intentional and, for better or worse, matches the way `InetAddress` chooses to handle these. There's a pretty long [section in the class Javadoc](https://github.com/google/guava/blob/master/guava/src/com/google/common/net/InetAddresses.java#L70) specifically addressing this behavior.

title: Immutable array list wrappers could return primitive iterators
body:
### API(s)

```java
ImmutableIntArray.of(1, 2, 3).asList().iterator(); // could return PrimitiveIterator.OfInt

ImmutableLongArray.of(1, 2, 3).asList().iterator(); // could return PrimitiveIterator.OfLong

ImmutableDoubleArray.of(1.0, 2.0, 3.0).asList().iterator(); // could return PrimitiveIterator.OfDouble
```

### How do you want it to be improved?

ImmutableIntArray et al have list wrappers (AsList); they already return primitive spliterators, however their iterator methods could also return their respective PrimitiveIterator class.

### Why do we need it to be improved?

Overriding the default iterator method to return a PrimitiveIterator may help with legacy APIs that accept `List<Integer>`, etc. Places where the method signature itself is hard to change could instead check for the presence of a PrimitiveIterator to avoid boxing while iterating over such a List.

### Example

```java
// Unfortunate API that accepts List<Double>
public void process(List<Double> scores) {
    Iterator<Double> iterator = scores.iterator();
    if (iterator instanceof PrimitiveIterator.OfDouble pi) {
       while (pi.hasNext()) {
           pi.nextDouble(); // access primitive value without boxing
       }
    }
    // ...
}
```

### Current Behavior

The current List wrappers incur boxing overhead, and don't provide a mechanism to iterate without boxing apart from getting the spliterator directly and casting to Spliterator.OfDouble, etc.

### Desired Behavior

Easier mechanism to iterate over the list wrapper without boxing.

### Concrete Use Cases

Attempting to update legacy APIs that accept types such as `List<Double>` to use `ImmutableDoubleArray` directly is more difficult than changing the code to check for PrimitiveIterator support at runtime.

- [x] I have read and understood the [contribution guidelines](https://github.com/google/guava/wiki/HowToContribute#feature-requests).

- [x] I have read and understood [Guava's philosophy](https://github.com/google/guava/wiki/PhilosophyExplained), and I strongly believe that this proposal aligns with it.

title: Prepare Guava for JEP 500 ("Prepare to Make Final Mean Final")
body:
The problem I'm aware of at the moment is with `Serialization.getFieldSetter`. It is used from:

- `ConcurrentHashMultiset`
- `ImmutableMultimap`
- `ImmutableSetMultimap`
- `TreeMultiset`

I hacked up `pom.xml` to have its Surefire `argLine`  contain `--illegal-final-field-mutation=deny`. Then I grabbed a `jdk-26-ea+25`, configured it as a `<version>26-ea</version>` in my `.m2/toolchains.xml` (because it [needs to be "configured," not just "discovered"](https://gemini.google.com/share/96a883c0c550)), and ran tests with it (in a victory for https://github.com/google/guava/commit/c171b9cbb86cc3d17dea6838d0c146e7bb45fc9b):

```shell
$ JAVA_HOME=/usr/local/google/home/cpovirk/jdk-26-ea+25 ./mvnw clean install -Dmaven.javadoc.skip -Dtoolchain.skip -Dsurefire.toolchain.version=26-ea
```

The resulting failures are many (over 10k), but that's because our test-suite builders attempt to perform a huge number of tests on reserialized collections, so a deserialization failure breaks them all. All the failures trace to three fields:

- `AbstractSortedMultiset.comparator`
- `ConcurrentHashMultiset.countMap`
- `ImmutableMultimap.map`

I think the four hits from my `Serialization.getFieldSetter` search are more accurate: The code fails at runtime on the first field that it tries to set, so we don't get far enough to see the field specific to `ImmutableSetMultimap`.

comments.body:
On `ConcurrentHashMultiset` and maybe the `Immutable*Multiset` classes:

I had some hope that [the `ConcurrentHashMultiset` custom serialization code](https://github.com/google/guava/blob/5b1d8b11d413068cf2ebb70cf194ae2f644bc90a/guava/src/com/google/common/collect/ConcurrentHashMultiset.java#L593-L608) was exactly equivalent to default Java serialization, which [will continue to work, even with `final` fields, after the work started in JEP 500](https://openjdk.org/jeps/500#:~:text=Serialization%20libraries%20should%20use%20sun.reflect.ReflectionFactory). (The code has been through a series of changes, notably in cl/7789252 and cl/16975467, so it could easily have ended up reinventing the default in a complex way.) And at least some of our other classes may be similar (though not `TreeMultiset`).

However, it sounds like the default Java serialized form would contain the field name, too, while we don't. Guava [reserves the right to change serialized forms](https://github.com/google/guava?tab=readme-ov-file#important-warnings), and it has done so in the past, and _maybe_ such a change is even somehow safe for users who depend on deserializing older forms with newer versions? But we'd apparently be making some kind of change, so we'd want to do that with our eyes open.

The right way to set `final` fields during deserialization is with `ReflectionFactory`, as covered in the JEP. I got some working code for that for a toy example from Gemini. Complications there include:

- We would need different code for Android and JRE (for `guava-android`) and for different JRE versions (since the relevant `ReflectionFactory` APIs were added only in Java 24, I think?).
- ~I think users would need to set `--add-opens java.base/sun.reflect=ALL-UNNAMED` or `--add-opens java.base/sun.reflect=com.google.common` (depending on whether Guava is on the classpath or module path).~ \[edit: No, Gemini had suggested this in a code comment, and I'd found that it was incorrect, but I'd forgotten to go back and remove the comment from the prototype code.\]
- I'd want to understand better whether that's a recommended path forward for _authors of libraries with `Serializable` types_ or just for _authors of serialization libraries capable of serializing arbitrary objects_. Presumably the best move is to avoid having to set `final` fields at all. (I'd prefer that we find a solution that isn't "Make the fields non-`final`," though, especially for the immutable collections, given concerns like maximizing thread safety.)

In my opinion, we should rewrite the serialization of these classes so that it uses either default serialization or serial proxies. Switching to use `sun.reflect.ReflectionFactory` just seems like kicking the problem down the road. We have always explicitly disclaimed support for serial compatibility across releases, so people should not be depending on it. We might even find some use for `serialVersionUID`!

For `ConcurrentHashMultiset` in particular, I don't see any reason other than serial compatibility why we couldn't just use default serialization. I dug up the change from 2008 that introduced the use of `Field.setAccessible`, and its description simply said "ConcurrentMultiset uses same serialized forms as other multisets". OK, but why? Why do we care? It's not as if you can serialize as one kind of multiset and deserialize as another.

Thanks. Do you feel any better about the approach that uses `deserializationReplacement`?

I agree that default serialization or a serialization proxy is the Correct solution, but I know we got bit the last time we tried to fix a questionable serialized form (cl/324749502, cl/326086350), so I'd be happy to chicken out and do the more compatible thing, since it's likely not much harder than doing the Correct thing.

I guess those citations suggest that we are stuck with the current serial forms, despite our explicitly having told people not to rely on them. I'm basically OK with any solution that doesn't require modifying final fields.

We have a change in flight for `ConcurrentHashMultiset` that uses the `deserializationReplacement` approach, and it looks like that will be good enough to finish and then apply to the other types.

In hindsight, I think that the `sun.reflect.ReflectionFactory` approach was a red herring: I had looked into it a couple months prior out of curiosity about what serialization libraries were supposed to do. That left it fresh enough in my mind that I thought of it here but not fresh enough that I realized it wasn't the right tool: I think `ReflectionFactory` is more about giving _other_ reflection libraries the same capabilities as Java reflection, not about enabling Java reflection to set `final` fields in any way other than the way it already does for non-`transient` fields. That means it's of no help here, where our problem is precisely that we need to set `final transient` fields.

([The JEP](https://openjdk.org/jeps/500) could perhaps be clearer on this, but I grant that `final transient` fields + `readObject` + `get(Declared)Field` + `setAccessible` is an extremely unusual combination, one that I see in Google's monorepo outside Guava and the JDK in only `org.geotools.coverage.grid.GridCoverage2D` and `org.apache.commons.math3.linear.MatrixUtils` (also cloned into `org.hipparchus.linear.MatrixUtils`)—and possibly not even the latest version of all those classes.)

> I dug up the change from 2008 that introduced the use of `Field.setAccessible`, and its description simply said "ConcurrentMultiset uses same serialized forms as other multisets". OK, but why? Why do we care? It's not as if you can serialize as one kind of multiset and deserialize as another.

That belatedly got me wondering: How do the other multisets handle this problem?

The answer: `AbstractMapBasedMultiset` (used by `HashMultiset` and `LinkedHashMultiset`) [still uses a non-`final` field for `backingMap`](https://github.com/google/guava/blob/8240c7e5963ee69464e870603d2e0dac06726ebb/guava/src/com/google/common/collect/AbstractMapBasedMultiset.java#L54) so that it can continue to set the field during deserialization. Similarly, `EnumMultiset` has [a whole mess of non-`final` fields](https://github.com/google/guava/blob/8240c7e5963ee69464e870603d2e0dac06726ebb/guava/src/com/google/common/collect/EnumMultiset.java#L86-L90) for the same reason.

So it would probably be defensible to do the same for `ConcurentHashMultiset` and especially `TreeMultiset`. (Alternatively, it would be defensible to argue that we should make the fields in `AbstractMapBasedMultiset` and `EnumMultiset` be `final`, too, updating serialization accordingly. But I'd rather do what we need to for the JEP and then stop thinking about serialization again for as long as possible :) So the only question I'd ask is what to do for the multisets we're touching now.)

And: As you've noted in the review for my upcoming change to `TreeMultiset`, it is _way_ better to just use the constructor there like a normal human being. I'd say that's true even if we were setting the fields normally, since we still end up having to recreate the constructor's logic. title: Entry set spliterators don't report the DISTINCT characteristic
body:
### Guava Version

33.5.0-jre

### Description

I noticed a minor issue with some of the entry set spliterators not consistently reporting DISTINCT (ImmutableMap, ImmutableBiMap, etc). This is because they are backed by an ImmutableList, but we could easily override the characteristics of the Spliterator since it is known to be distinct.

### Example

```java
ImmutableBiMap.of().entrySet().spliterator().hasCharacteristics(Spliterator.DISTINCT); // true
ImmutableBiMap.of("a", "b").entrySet().spliterator().hasCharacteristics(Spliterator.DISTINCT); // false
ImmutableBiMap.of("a", "b", "c", "d").entrySet().spliterator().hasCharacteristics(Spliterator.DISTINCT); // false
ImmutableMap.of().entrySet().spliterator().hasCharacteristics(Spliterator.DISTINCT); // false
ImmutableMap.of("a", "b").entrySet().spliterator().hasCharacteristics(Spliterator.DISTINCT)) // false
ImmutableMap.of("a", "b", "c", "d").entrySet().spliterator().hasCharacteristics(Spliterator.DISTINCT); // false


Contrast that with the JDK:


Map.of().entrySet().spliterator().hasCharacteristics(Spliterator.DISTINCT); // true
Map.of("a", "b").entrySet().spliterator().hasCharacteristics(Spliterator.DISTINCT); // true
Map.of("a", "b", "c", "d").entrySet().spliterator().hasCharacteristics(Spliterator.DISTINCT); // true
Map.of("a", "b", "c", "d", "e", "f").entrySet().spliterator().hasCharacteristics(Spliterator.DISTINCT); // true
```

### Expected Behavior

I would expect the spliterator characteristics to match the JDK and report DISTINCT for an entry set.

### Actual Behavior

Entry set spliterators don't consistently report DISTINCT.

### Packages

com.google.common.collect

### Platforms

_No response_

- [x] I agree to follow the [code of conduct](https://github.com/google/.github/blob/master/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

- [x] I can reproduce the bug with the [latest](https://github.com/google/guava/releases/latest) version of Guava available.

comments.body: Under what circumstances does this produce any difference in semantics or performance, though?  I believe we considered this at the time, but concluded that it was only relevant someone called `distinct()` on a stream directly from a set, which seemed unlikely.

> Under what circumstances does this produce any difference in semantics or performance, though? I believe we considered this at the time, but concluded that it was only relevant someone called `distinct()` on a stream directly from a set, which seemed unlikely.

Right, I believe it would disable optimizations if someone called `distinct()`, but I don't know that it's all that far-fetched that it could occur, basically when the stream interaction is far removed (a method that accepts a Collection that then does some stream manipulation, something like that).

I think the main thing here is just the consistency, I noticed the discrepancy between the JDK behavior and Guava, and it seems relatively easy to just set the correct characteristics.
The Javadoc for Set also indicates that the spliterator reports DISTINCT.

I think we've previously discussed characteristics like [`NONNULL`, `CONCURRENT`](https://github.com/google/guava/issues/7855), and `ORDERED` (internal issue 215153860, "Without it, `distinct` discards ordering."). It seems that we're not necessarily especially careful about our characteristics, probably because of the lack of clear impact. It might be nice to fix (so thank you for reporting) but probably wouldn't be a priority.
It is trivial to fix, would you be inclined to accept a PR for this?

Another argument in favor of this change is that it seems that in many other places in Guava, we do go out of our way to set DISTINCT for sets / entry sets, so this seems like an inconsistency (AbstractMultimap, CompactHashMap, ArrayTable, etc).

Thanks. I think @lowasser is looking some at this, but I don't want to make promises about specifically what that will amount to, nor around whatever might be left. Hopefully we can figure that out afterward.

I have been trying to wrap my head around this for some time now (without success), and I can't find a test case that covers this.

My recollection is that this was added in one of my first bug fixes when learning that code. The original author was on sabbatical and no one else knew the code very well, but a commonly reported footgun were deadlocks in production due to recursive loads. I didn't want to use a ThreadLocal because those had a reputation for performance issues (multiple rewrites). The alternative was to stash the thread id in the loading entry as extra bookkeeping, but that needed care for proper clean up. I advocated for the holdsLock trick because an uncontended lock is free, it had no extra memory (header bit), there were no observed degradations, and it was a very low risk change to unfamiliar code. We then unofficially supported recursive loads despite discouraging them, and future discussions wrt ConcurrentHashMap facing the same problem. (My name might not be on the internal commit bit due to my manager having preferred that our team ships CLs to others to avoid perceptions that 20% projects might distract from the core project's timeline)

Virtual thread support in mutexes is on going work ([latest status](https://youtu.be/WoQJnnMIlFY?t=421)). It may have been premature to have released the feature in Java 21 without it, as it is [very easy](https://mail.openjdk.org/pipermail/loom-dev/2023-July/005993.html) to deadlock in JDK only code due to ample usage of synchronization throughout the standard library. The answer isn't to remove all of that and switching to `ReentrantLock` was only meant as advice for those wanting to experiment for feedback purposes. I wouldn't use VTs in production until these footguns are resolved, which will likely happen before most are ready to upgrade to 21 anyway. 

I still stand by my position in Caffeine that it is not worth the effort and instead the JDK team will solve it soonish. It is good to be aware of, but primarily as a reason to avoid adoption of VTs until they are more robust.

Even though It pains me a bit to be using a `ThreadLocal`, I think in this case, since we can just clean everything up inside the [finally](https://github.com/google/guava/blob/4f12c5891a7adedbaa1d99fc9f77d8cc4e9da206/guava/src/com/google/common/cache/LocalCache.java#L2194) this should really be manageable (`ThreadLocal` creation and destruction would only be ~10 loc apart). Unlike I said yesterday though I didn't put a static object inside the `ThreadLocal` but the entry itself, because otherwise we would also fail on the (maybe a bit weird) legal case that someone tries to load a different key in their loader. 

An edgecase that this implementation would not detect is if one tries to recursively load the same entry, but with another "normal" loader in the middle. In that case the threadlocal would be reset by the second loader, and the third one could no longer determine that loader nr. 1 already tried to load this entry. But this really seems very niche to me.  

I also wrote a test for it. Please do let me know If you would like me to submit a PR, or if you have other suggestions or comments.

Unfortunately circular recursive calls (a -> b -> a) is not unheard of for longer dependency chains. The recursion is rarely intentional but rather a side-effect of calling an application api that circles back eventually. A fast fail is much better than a deadlock since the developer won’t understand at first what went wrong.

Thus, the ThreadLocal would need to capture the list of loading entries. That’s still not horrible or difficult to implement. 

Alternatively the loading reference entry would need to capture the thread. This entry type is temporary and swapped out once complete. That would avoid the entry copying concerns that the doc comment mentions since the copy could capture the thread as needed. This is probably the ideal approach, just a bit more work and think time to avoid regressions.

If you can use Caffeine, then AsyncCache is compatible as it defers the compute to a future so the monitor is held briefly for establishing the mapping. The executor could be set to a VT and the synchronous view used for convenience.

Those changes look good. From a quick review it doesn't seem this entry type needs to be copied (`copyEntry` / `copyFor` return itself) so presumably the original doc comment may have been an incorrect concern. Caffeine is mostly a drop-in replacement for Guava's cache with minor [differences](https://github.com/ben-manes/caffeine/wiki/Guava). The performance difference can be quite stark, see below for a zipfian workload on my macbook with 16 threads and varying Guava's concurrencyLevel (defaults to 4). Whether that translates to realizable gains is application specific, so you might consider capturing a jfr profile to see if the caches remain a bottleneck after your fix.

Ok great. Can I open a PR for this now?

Cool. A migration to Caffeine is definitely on our radar and will happen at some point.
No guarantees, but I'd say that opening a PR is likely to be worth your time. I can have a look at it and run some tests. Thanks.

Resetting a completed HTTP/1.1 request closes a pooled connection after reuse
body:
### Version

4.4.1, 4.5.31

### Context

An HTTP/1.1 HttpClientRequest can retain access to its former connection after the request has completed. If the connection returns to the pool and is assigned to a newer request, calling reset() on the completed request closes the physical connection now serving the newer request.

Expected behavior

Calling reset() on an already completed request should be a no-op and must not affect a subsequent request using the pooled connection.

Actual behavior

The subsequent request fails with io.vertx.core.http.HttpClosedException: Connection was closed.

Probable cause

Http1xClientConnection.reset() uses responses.contains(stream) || stream.responseEnded to decide that a stream is in flight. responseEnded remains true after a completed stream has left the connection tracking queues. A late reset therefore marks the physical connection for closure after it has been reused.

The attached focused Http1xTest uses one keep-alive connection with pipelining disabled. Request A completes, Request B reuses the connection, and reset() is called on A while B is active. Expect: 100-continue makes the sequence deterministic; the underlying issue is not specific to 100 Continue.

Environment: macOS 26.5.2, OpenJDK 17.0.19.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Check out the Vert.x 4.5.31 tag.
2. Apply the attached test patch.
3. Run: mvn -Dtest=io.vertx.core.http.Http1xTest#testResetCompletedRequestDoesNotCloseReusedExpectContinueRequest test
4. Observe that the test fails with HttpClosedException: Connection was closed.

The equivalent behavior passes on the 4.2.6 code line and fails on the 4.4.1 and 4.5.31 code lines.

title: acceptHandshake blocks 10s waiting on a task it queued to its own executor (worker context), and the failure is unreportable
body:
### Version

5.1.4 (regression; not present in 4.5.13)

### Context

Environment: vertx-core 5.1.4, Java 21.0.6, Linux x86_64.

On a `ThreadingModel.WORKER` verticle, `HttpServerRequest.toWebSocket()` can block its carrier thread for exactly 10s and then fail. It waits on a task it has just scheduled onto the context that is currently executing it — on a serialized executor that task cannot run until the wait returns.

The only symptom in the logs is a secondary `IllegalStateException: Response head already sent`; the real cause is discarded. Both problems are inside vertx-core — the application only calls `toWebSocket()`.

## Defect 1 — self-deadlock

`Http1ServerRequest.toWebSocket()` is internally `webSocketHandshake().compose(h -> h.accept())`. When that continuation is not inline it is delivered as a `FutureBase$EmitResultTask` through the context executor, so `accept()` runs *as a task on the serialized `TaskQueue`*.

`ServerWebSocketHandshaker.acceptHandshake()`, bytecode offsets in 5.1.4:

```
 58: WebSocketServerHandshaker.handshake(...)   // writes the 101
 64: Http1ServerResponse.completeHandshake()    // head COMMITTED
137: ContextInternal.execute(Runnable)          // queues the Netty pipeline swap
150: CompletableFuture.get(10, SECONDS)         // blocks waiting for the task queued at 137
159: new RuntimeException(cause)                // on timeout
```

`ContextBase.execute(Runnable)` runs inline only `if (executor().inThread())`, otherwise it enqueues. `WorkerExecutor.inThread()` is a per-executor `ThreadLocal`, so from within an `EmitResultTask` it takes the enqueue branch — appending the pipeline swap behind the task that is about to block on it.

The 10s value is a literal with no config key. Every observed failure consumed the *full* timeout (measured 10.003s and 10.069s), which is what distinguishes this from a race.

## Defect 2 — the error cannot report itself

The head is committed at offset **64**; the failure happens at **150**. `accept()` catches it and calls `rejectHandshake(BAD_REQUEST)` → `setStatusCode()` on an already-committed response:

```
java.lang.IllegalStateException: Response head already sent
    at io.vertx.core.http.impl.HttpServerResponseImpl.checkHeadWritten(HttpServerResponseImpl.java:120)
    at io.vertx.core.http.impl.HttpServerResponseImpl.setStatusCode(HttpServerResponseImpl.java:148)
```

The timeout `RuntimeException` is lost. **This stands independently of the threading issue** — any failure occurring between the commit point and the reject is currently unreportable.

## Observed stack

Captured live while blocked, via `jcmd Thread.print`:

```
"wp.APIServer.1-0"  java.lang.Thread.State: TIMED_WAITING (parking)
    at java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture.timedGet(java.base@21.0.6)
    at java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture.get(java.base@21.0.6)
    at io.vertx.core.http.impl.websocket.ServerWebSocketHandshaker.acceptHandshake(ServerWebSocketHandshaker.java:209)
    at io.vertx.core.http.impl.websocket.ServerWebSocketHandshaker.accept(ServerWebSocketHandshaker.java:106)
    at io.vertx.core.http.impl.http1.Http1ServerRequest.lambda$toWebSocket$0(Http1ServerRequest.java:414)
    at io.vertx.core.impl.future.Composition.complete(Composition.java:40)
    at io.vertx.core.impl.future.FutureBase$EmitResultTask.run(FutureBase.java:125)
    at io.vertx.core.impl.WorkerExecutor$1.execute(WorkerExecutor.java:68)
    at io.vertx.core.impl.WorkerTask.run(WorkerTask.java:57)
    at io.vertx.core.impl.TaskQueue.run(TaskQueue.java:86)
```

`Composition.complete` → `EmitResultTask` → `TaskQueue.run` is the point: the handshake is running as a queued continuation, not inline. Two dumps taken 2s apart held different `CompletableFuture$Signaller` instances, so these are separate handshakes each blocking rather than one long wait.

## 4.5.13 for comparison

`Http1xServerConnection`, `ServerWebSocketImpl` and `Http1xServerRequest` in 4.5.13 contain **zero** `CompletableFuture.get`/`await`. `doHandshake()` commits *after* a successful handshake and removes the pipeline handler inline; `createWebSocket()` is fully promise-based. Both regressions arrived together: the commit point moved ahead of the failure point, and an inline pipeline swap became a cross-thread dispatch plus a blocking wait.

## Impact

WebSocket upgrades intermittently stall for 10s and then fail, so a SockJS event-bus bridge never connects and the application appears to hang rather than error. Measured on one server: 76 failed upgrades in ~35 minutes of normal traffic; zero on the same build with the verticle deployed as `EVENT_LOOP`.

`setWorkerPoolSize(N)` does not help — a verticle instance is serialized by its `TaskQueue` regardless of pool size.

## Calling code

Reduced from the application where this occurs. The only Vert.x entry point involved is `request.toWebSocket()`, reached through `SockJSHandler`.

Deployment — N instances, each with its own single-thread worker pool:

```java
for (int i = 0; i < instances; i++) {                       // 4 in our deployment
    vertx.deployVerticle(new ApiServerVerticle(), new DeploymentOptions()
            .setThreadingModel(ThreadingModel.WORKER)
            .setWorkerPoolSize(1)
            .setWorkerPoolName("wp.APIServer." + i));
}
```

Route — SockJS event-bus bridge, WEBSOCKET the only enabled transport:

```java
Router router = Router.router(vertx);

SockJSHandler sockJs = SockJSHandler.create(vertx, new SockJSHandlerOptions()
        .setHeartbeatInterval(60000)
        .addDisabledTransport(Transport.XHR.name())
        .addDisabledTransport(Transport.JSON_P.name())
        .addDisabledTransport(Transport.EVENT_SOURCE.name())
        .addDisabledTransport(Transport.HTML_FILE.name()));

router.route("/eventbus/*")
        .handler(CorsHandler.create())
        .failureHandler(ctx -> {
            // guarded, because the upgrade completes asynchronously and ending an
            // already-ended response here throws "Response head already sent" as well
            if (!ctx.response().ended()) {
                ctx.response().setStatusCode(ctx.statusCode() > 0 ? ctx.statusCode() : 403).end();
            }
        })
        .subRouter(sockJs.bridge(new SockJSBridgeOptions()
                .addInboundPermitted(new PermittedOptions().setAddress("server"))
                .addOutboundPermitted(new PermittedOptions().setAddressRegex("user\\..*"))));

vertx.createHttpServer(new HttpServerOptions().setSsl(true))
        .requestHandler(router)
        .listen(443);
```

`SockJSHandler`'s WebSocket transport calls `routingContext.request().toWebSocket()`, which is where the stack above originates.

Full thread dumps available on request.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Deploy a verticle with `ThreadingModel.WORKER`, `setWorkerPoolSize(1)`, a named worker pool, and several instances (reproduced with 4).
2. Have it serve a SockJS event-bus bridge with only the WEBSOCKET transport enabled (see "Calling code" above).
3. Drive WebSocket upgrades against `/eventbus/websocket` concurrently with other HTTP traffic.
4. Upgrades intermittently stall for exactly 10s, then fail with `IllegalStateException: Response head already sent`. A thread dump taken during the stall shows the carrier thread parked in `CompletableFuture.timedGet` inside `ServerWebSocketHandshaker.acceptHandshake`.

Note on reproducing this: the trigger is `webSocketHandshake()` completing asynchronously, so that `.compose(...)` delivers the continuation via `FutureBase$EmitResultTask` rather than running it inline. Under light synthetic load the future is usually already complete, the continuation runs inline, `inThread()` is true, the pipeline swap executes immediately and nothing blocks — a standalone harness driving 2,000 upgrades at 25-way concurrency did **not** reproduce it. It reproduces reliably under real mixed traffic.

### Do you have a reproducer?

_No response_

## On "deadlock": I overstated it

I claimed a deterministic self-deadlock. I can't support that, and I withdraw it.

## What I can still show

The wait itself is real and unconditional in 5.1.4. `ServerWebSocketHandshaker.acceptHandshake()`:

```
 64: Http1ServerResponse.completeHandshake()   // response head COMMITTED
113: new CompletableFuture
137: ContextInternal.execute(Runnable)         // queues the Netty pipeline swap
144: ldc2_w 10L
147: TimeUnit.SECONDS
150: CompletableFuture.get(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS)   // blocks; hardcoded, no config key
168: athrow RuntimeException
```

And in production it demonstrably does block. Captured mid-hang, unchanged across three dumps 5s apart, CPU frozen:

```
"wp.APIServer.0-0" TIMED_WAITING
  java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture.timedGet
  io.vertx.core.http.impl.websocket.ServerWebSocketHandshaker.acceptHandshake(...:209)
  io.vertx.core.internal.concurrent.TaskQueue.run(TaskQueue.java:86)
```

So the caller is running as a queued task on a serialized `TaskQueue` and is blocked inside the 10s wait. What my reproducer has not yet isolated is the configuration in which `execute()` dispatches cross-thread rather than inline. Our server reaches this path through **vertx-web's `SockJSHandler`** rather than a raw `webSocketHandler`, and I suspect that is the difference. I'll follow up if I can reduce it.

Field data from that build, for whatever it's worth as a signal rather than a proof:

- 76 failed upgrades in ~35 minutes; **every one consumed the full timeout** (gaps of 10.003s, 10.069s) — none completed late, which is what made me reach for "deadlock"
- An A/B on two otherwise-identical servers under comparable load: EVENT_LOOP **0** failures, WORKER **12**; moving the WORKER box to EVENT_LOOP took it to **0** on the same host
- `setWorkerPoolSize(N)` made no difference, as expected — a verticle instance is serialized by `TaskQueue` regardless of pool size

Whether the right label is starvation or something structural, a hardcoded 10s blocking wait with no configuration key inside `accept()` is fragile: it converts any period where the target context is unavailable into a failed upgrade. Our event loops were measurably unavailable for multi-second stretches (a 6s JDBC `isValid()` on the loop, gzip `Deflater` on the loop, a 916ms allocation Full GC) — all our own bugs, but the handshake is what surfaced them, and it surfaced them unreportably.

## Defect 2 — what response is actually sent

You asked what the client receives. My reproducer answers this directly, and I think it's the more serious half.

The `101` is written **and flushed before the wait begins**. In the run above the client had `HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols` in hand at **t=0.10s**, while the server-side handler completed later. `completeHandshake()` at offset 64 commits the head; the `execute()`/`get()` pair at 137–150 comes after.

So on failure:

1. the client has already been told **`101 Switching Protocols`** — the upgrade succeeded
2. the pipeline swap never happens, so the channel still has the HTTP codec, not the WebSocket codec
3. `accept()` catches the timeout and calls `rejectHandshake()` → `setStatusCode()` → `IllegalStateException: Response head already sent`

There is no error response, and there **cannot** be one — the `101` is on the wire. The client holds a socket it believes is an open WebSocket and which will never carry a frame. That is why our logs showed 4153 `Response head already sent` lines naming no cause: the `IllegalStateException` is the aftermath of the real failure, not the failure.

For contrast, 4.5.13 ordered it the other way round and had a working error path:

```java
try { handshaker.handshake(...); }
catch (Exception e) { response.setStatusCode(BAD_REQUEST).end(); throw e; }  // reportable
response.completeHandshake();                                                // commit AFTER success
ChannelPipeline pipeline = channel.pipeline();
if (handler != null) pipeline.remove(handler);                               // inline, no wait
```

Two independent changes in 5.x: the commit point moved *before* the new failure point, and an inline pipeline swap became a dispatch plus a blocking wait. The first is a defect regardless of what we conclude about the second, and it's the one I'd most like to see addressed — it makes every failure in this method self-concealing.

## Reproducer

```
mvn -q compile exec:java -Dexec.args="WORKER 0"          # idle loop      -> succeeds ~0.10s
mvn -q compile exec:java -Dexec.args="WORKER 12000"      # loop blocked   -> succeeds at 12.1s
mvn -q compile exec:java -Dexec.args="EVENT_LOOP 12000"  # control
```

Raw-socket client so the exact bytes and their arrival times are visible. Happy to extend it toward the SockJS path if that's the useful next step.

In Quarkus, we switched from HttpServerOptions to HttpServerConfig (to handle HTTP/3).

title: HttpClient with a LoadBalancer uses only one IP for a multi-homed host
body:
### Version

5.1.2

### Context

An `HttpClient` configured with a `LoadBalancer` is designed to resolve **all** of a host's A-records and balance requests across them (`HttpClientImpl`: `resolveAll = loadBalancer != null`; `OriginResolver` builds an `OriginServer` per resolved IP, all `available`). In practice it connects to a **single** IP for a multi-homed host.

### Notes
- `((VertxInternal) vertx).nameResolver().resolveAll("www.google.com")` returns all 8 addresses, so DNS resolution is fine — the issue is downstream in the built-in origin-resolution → endpoint → `selectServer` path.
- Workaround: supplying an explicit `AddressResolver` (e.g. `AddressResolver.mappingResolver(...)` with the resolved IPs) + the same `LoadBalancer` **does** round-robin across all IPs. So only the built-in (no-custom-resolver) path is affected.

### Steps to reproduce

### Reproducer
```java
Vertx vertx = Vertx.vertx();
HttpClient client = vertx.httpClientBuilder()
    .with(new HttpClientOptions().setProtocolVersion(HttpVersion.HTTP_1_1).setSsl(true))
    .withLoadBalancer(LoadBalancer.ROUND_ROBIN)   // no custom AddressResolver
    .build();

Set<String> ips = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();
CountDownLatch latch = new CountDownLatch(24);
for (int i = 0; i < 24; i++) {
  client.request(new RequestOptions().setMethod(HttpMethod.GET)
          .setHost("www.google.com").setPort(443).setURI("/").setSsl(true))   // 8 A-records
      .compose(req -> req.send().compose(HttpClientResponse::body).map(b -> req.connection()))
      .onComplete(ar -> { if (ar.succeeded()) ips.add(ar.result().remoteAddress().hostAddress()); latch.countDown(); });
}
latch.await(40, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
System.out.println("distinct remote IPs = " + ips.size());   // prints 1, despite 8 A-records
```

### Expected
Requests spread across the host's resolved IPs per the policy (≈8 distinct remote IPs).

### Actual
All requests hit one IP. Same with `ROUND_ROBIN`, `RANDOM`, and `LEAST_REQUESTS` — and `RANDOM` is stateless, so the load balancer is selecting among a *single* server; the resolved address set never reaches the selector.

To be fair, the inflation shouldn't happen just once in the lifetime of the monitor to be inflated, but still, this is not good.
Ideally we should just avoid to make it happen, since it shuldn't.

This is what I can see in Quarkus: Profiled with async-profiler `-e lock` on JDK 25, Quarkus 3.34.2 (Vert.x 4.5.26), 4 CPUs, 100 connections: - `interruptLock` (EPollSelectorImpl.clearInterrupt): **1,062 ms** wait on event loops in 10s - `Http1xServerConnection` (ConnectionBase.queueForWrite lambda): **586 ms** wait on event loops in 10s The connection monitor is acquired by `VertxOutputStream.write()` ([source](https://github.com/quarkusio/quarkus/blob/23faec4af107387f532447419b54c40495153311/independent-projects/vertx-utils/src/main/java/io/quarkus/vertx/utils/VertxOutputStream.java#L84)) before calling `response.write()`, and held across the entire wakeup chain including syscalls: ``` VT carrier: Event loop: ───────────────────────────────────── ───────────────────────────────────── 1. synchronized(connection) (sleeping in epoll_wait) 2. awaitWriteable() 3. response.write(buf) 4. → writeToChannel() 5. → synchronized(this) [reentrant] 6. → queueForWrite() 7. → writeInProgress++ 8. → execute(lambda) 9. → wakeup() 10. → synchronized(interruptLock) 11. → eventfd.set() ──────→ epoll_wait returns 12. → monitorexit(interruptLock) processEvents() clearInterrupt() → synchronized(interruptLock) ← MAY CONTEND → eventfd.reset() runAllTasks() → queueForWrite lambda 13. → monitorexit(this) [reentrant] → synchronized(connection) ← BLOCKS HERE 14. monitorexit(connection) ──────────→ (unblocked, decrements writeInProgress) ``` `eventfd.set()` (step 11) wakes the event loop immediately, but the VT carrier still holds the connection monitor — it needs to complete `monitorexit(interruptLock)` (futex_wake syscall on the inflated monitor) before reaching step 14. The event loop is fast enough to wake, process the interrupt, and reach the connection lock before the carrier releases it. I think it is the same pattern observed by @barreiro some time ago which led to replacing the `synchronized` block (and getting it reverted). A simpler fix retaining the lock could be to use a lazy submission inside the syncronized block and a separate wakeup outside of it, to narrow the window where the 2 threads (VT and EventLoop one) could compete. i.e. using https://github.com/netty/netty/blob/4.1/common/src/main/java/io/netty/util/concurrent/SingleThreadEventExecutor.java#L821 But @cescoffier it means that Quarkus, which is synchronizing on the connection itself for writing, need to call itself the wakeup outside it.
perhaps from worker thread (loom) we should do differently and just do a simple schedule without trying to order message ? that way this flow would be used from non vertx thread only

title: Race condition in `HttpClientResponse.body()` / `end()`
body:
### Version

4.5.25, 5.0.8 (likely all 4.x and 5.x)

### Context

I've been investigating the very rare occurence of timeouts in some of my tests and could narrow it down to Vert.X HTTP response handling.

Note: instead of `.compose()`, `.flatMap()` or `.map()` work as well.

Additional question:
* Should `io.vertx.core.http.impl.HttpClientResponseImpl#eventHandler` be `volatile`?

A full reproducer is available in [this GitHub repo](https://github.com/snazy/vertx-body-race-reproducer).

## Summary

`HttpClientResponse.body()` (and `end()`) can permanently hang when used
in a `.compose()` chain after `HttpClient.request().compose(req -> req.send())`.
The `Future` returned by `body()` is never completed, causing the caller to
time out.

Affects **Vert.x 4.5.x** and **5.0.x**. Observed at a rate of about **0.01 %** per request on an idle system with loopback networking.

## Root cause

`HttpClientResponseImpl` lazily creates an internal `HttpEventHandler`
(which holds the `bodyPromise` / `endPromise`) the first time `body()`,
`end()`, `handler()`, or `endHandler()` is called.

`handleEnd(MultiMap)` — called when the response is fully received — reads
this field under `synchronized(conn)` and, if it is still `null`, **silently
does nothing**:

```java
// HttpClientResponseImpl (identical in Vert.x 4 and 5)
void handleEnd(MultiMap trailers) {
    HttpEventHandler handler;
    synchronized (conn) {
        this.trailers = trailers;
        handler = eventHandler;       // ← null if body() hasn't been called yet
    }
    if (handler != null) {
        handler.handleEnd();          // ← skipped!
    }
}
```

`body()` is **not** synchronized on `conn`:

```java
@Override
public Future<Buffer> body() {
    return eventHandler(true).body(); // creates eventHandler + bodyPromise
}
```

Inside `HttpEventHandler.handleEnd()`, the body promise is completed:

```java
void handleEnd() {
    // ...
    if (bodyPromise != null) {
        bodyPromise.tryComplete(body);
    }
    if (endPromise != null) {
        endPromise.tryComplete();
    }
}
```

### The race

When a caller writes:

```java
httpClient.request(options)
    .compose(req -> req.send())
    .compose(resp -> resp.body())   // body() called in a compose callback
    .timeout(3, SECONDS);
```

the following sequence can occur:

1. `req.send()` completes — the response `Future` resolves.
2. The `.compose(resp -> resp.body())` callback is **scheduled** on the
   Vert.x context but has not run yet.
3. Meanwhile, the Netty pipeline has already received the full response
   (for a 204: headers + `LastHttpContent`; for a small 200: headers +
   body chunk + `LastHttpContent` — all in one TCP segment on loopback).
4. `Http1xClientConnection` processes the response end →
   `stream.handleEnd()` → `InboundMessageQueue.write()`.
5. The `InboundMessageQueue` drains and calls
   `HttpClientResponseImpl.handleEnd()`.
6. `handleEnd()` reads `eventHandler` under `synchronized(conn)` — it is
   **`null`** because `body()` has not been called yet.
7. `handleEnd()` silently returns without completing any promise.
8. The `.compose` callback finally runs, calls `resp.body()`, which creates
   a **new** `eventHandler` with a fresh `bodyPromise`.
9. **`bodyPromise` is never completed** — `handleEnd()` already fired and
   will not fire again.
10. The caller times out.

### Why it is rare

Steps 2–8 must interleave in a specific order. With
`setEventLoopPoolSize(1)`, the event loop handles both the I/O completion
and the context task scheduling, making the window slightly wider. On
loopback, small responses arrive in a single read cycle, which increases
the chance that the `InboundMessageQueue` drains the end message before the
compose callback is dispatched.

## Affected response types

| Response | Reproducible? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 204 No Content (no body) | ✅ most frequent | Headers + `LastHttpContent` in one read cycle |
| 200 + small JSON body | ✅ less frequent | Headers + body + `LastHttpContent` in one TCP segment |
| 200 + large body | ❌ not observed | Body chunks arrive over multiple read cycles; `body()` is called before the last chunk |

## How to reproduce

```bash
# Against Vert.x 5 (default: 5.0.8):
./gradlew test --rerun

# Against Vert.x 4:
./gradlew test --rerun -PvertxVersion=4.5.25
```

The test runs 50 000 iterations × multiple HTTP methods. With
`setEventLoopPoolSize(1)`, it typically fails within a few thousand
requests. If not, rerun the tests a couple of times.

## Possible fix

`handleEnd()` should record that the response has ended (it already sets
`this.trailers`). A subsequent `body()` / `end()` call should check this
flag and immediately complete the promise with the (empty) buffered body.

Alternatively, `body()` could be synchronized on `conn` so that it cannot
race with `handleEnd()`, and `handleEnd()` could always create the
`eventHandler` if it is `null` (ensuring the promise exists before trying
to complete it).

- **Java**: 21

- **OS**: Linux 6.17.0-19-generic (amd64)

### Describe the feature

Implement a reasonable support for HTTP alternative services.

## Motivation

One possible HTTP/3 discovery mechanism is through Alternative Services, which Vert.x HTTP client do not support

## Implementation

Vert.x HTTP client associates an origin like concept (as in Web Origin Concept) to a shared client pool to the origin server.

Vert.x 5 introduced an address resolver, proper support of origin to socket address can be implemented with a custom resolver.

Such resolver can resolve an origin (which can be an address) to a server origin endpoint which can comprehend the first HTTP service discovered by DNS and the alternative services discovered via the alternative services mechanism.

The resolver already implements time based eviction and invalidation which are necessary to support this.

This goes beyond HTTP/3 since alternative services work for HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 as well, it also affects service discovery and load balancing.

More details are included in the README.md, along with all software versions and configuration files needed. However, **I fully agree that a Vert.x-only based reproducer could be beneficial. We are working on providing that and will upload it here as soon as it is ready**.


In the meantime, to illustrate our case, we have the following setup, which matches what the Envoy-based reproducer is doing:

1.	A Vert.x 4.5.x-based HTTP/2 client application. This is where the problem manifests, and in the reproducer it is represented by an included Java class that generates HTTP/2 cleartext requests using Vert.x.
2.	An Istio service mesh that distributes traffic, which for our purposes can be reduced to an Envoy proxy process acting as an HTTP/2 server and distributing traffic to some REST services also using HTTP/2. The Envoy proxy configuration is included.
3.	Backend REST services. Any HTTP/2 server should suffice here; in the reproducer, nghttp is used.

The core concept is that the Vert.x HTTP/2 client is sending traffic to a server (Envoy proxy) configured to gracefully close the HTTP/2 connection/session every N requests. In the reproducer, N is 100 requests.

We believe the issue may not be specifically with RESET handling but rather with GOAWAY handling. In fact, packet captures show no difference between the reproduction where the problem appears in the client and the successful reproduction.

Our suspicion is that changes introduced in the following pull requests might be related:

4.5.18 [Allow an HTTP/2 server to be protected against MadeYouReset · Pull Request #5674 · eclipse-vertx/vert.x](https://github.com/eclipse-vertx/vert.x/pull/5674)
5.0.3 [Allow an HTTP/2 server to be protected against MadeYouReset · Pull Request #5675 · eclipse-vertx/vert.x](https://github.com/eclipse-vertx/vert.x/pull/5675)

Specifically regarding changes in the class src/main/java/io/vertx/core/http/impl/Http2ConnectionBase.java:
•	For HTTP/2 server connections, the changes are appropriate since after a client sends a GOAWAY it should not start any new requests, so it is correct to protect a server against these new requests.
•	However, for HTTP/2 client connections, according to the RFC, a server that is gracefully closing a connection should send a GOAWAY with last-stream-id equal to 2^31-1 and NO_ERROR, indicating its commitment to finish previously received requests before finally closing the connection. We suspect that for a Vert.x HTTP/2 client connection, with the latest changes in Http2ConnectionBase, since the client side of the connection shares the same code, when a completed request after a GOAWAY is received from the server side, that response is treated as an anomalous situation (GOAWAY error code = 0) and is not processed. This might be too strict since these requests were actually initiated by the client and when the response is received, it is rejecting them. A better approach for the client connection might be to accept responses for stream IDs the client has actually initiated and is waiting to complete and are within the last-stream-id received from server GOAWAY.

As mentioned, we are working on a Vert.x-only based reproduction.

Many thanks for your time and interest in this issue.

title: `JsonArray.contains(JsonObject / JsonArray)` returns `false`, in case `JsonObject` / `JsonArray` is represented as `Map` / `List` internally
body:
If you want to check whether a `JsonArray` contains a certain `JsonObject` or other `JsonArray` you may wrongly assume you can use the `contains` method. However as sometimes a `JsonObject` / `JsonArray` is represented as a `Map` or `List` in the internal `JsonArray` list, `contains` might return `false` even though semantically it should return `true`. Minimal reproducible example:

```java
JsonArray jsonArray = new JsonArray("[{\"foo\":\"bar\"}]");
System.out.println(jsonArray.contains(new JsonObject().put("foo", "bar"))); // false

System.out.println(jsonArray.contains(new JsonObject().put("foo", "bar").getMap())); // true
System.out.println(jsonArray.stream().anyMatch(obj -> obj.equals(new JsonObject().put("foo", "bar")))); // true
```

My assumption would be that the `contains` function behaves similarly to the `contains` function of the `List` interface, where it is documented that it returns `true` in case:

> Returns true if this list contains the specified element. More formally, returns true if and only if this list contains at least one element e such that (o==null ? e==null : o.equals(e)).

Which is not the case for the `contains` function of the `JsonArray`. So I would suggest this should be either treated as a bug, or the behaviour should be documented in the JavaDoc of the `contains` function.

title: Memory optimization
body:
There is a memory optimization that can be used in Vert.x in several places.
For example, here: 
`io.vertx.core.impl.VertxImpl.InternalTimerHandler`
`private final AtomicBoolean disposed = new AtomicBoolean();`
`AtomicBoolean` is quite a heavy object (many times bigger than volatile boolean)
It can be replaced with `VarHandle`. The `VarHandle` has all the same operations, but it is a static field member of a class and in object there is only a volatile byte or int field. You can see this technic in JDK 
`java.util.concurrent.FutureTask#set`

Replacing `Atomic`* with `VarHandle` and `volatile` in libraries makes sense.
It dramatically reduces the memory footprint without disadvantages.


I could make a PR for InternalTimerHandler.

thanks for reporting this issue, it raises a few concerns with respect to HTTP/2 upgrade:

The HTTP/2 RFC specs mandates the following items

1. `Requests that contain a payload body MUST be sent in their entirety before the client can send HTTP/2 frames.` 
2. `The HTTP/1.1 request that is sent prior to upgrade is assigned a stream identifier of 1 with default priority values.  Stream 1 is implicitly "half-closed" from the client toward the server, since the request is completed as an HTTP/1.1 request.`

From the Netty perspective, the stream is seen as _half closed remote_, since the stream cannot receive anymore frames from the HTTP/2 upgraded channel.

From the Vert.x perspective, the stream is seen as _open_ since the header frame is processed but the stream is not ended e.g the stream can contain a body and we expect content messages.

The test ends the response in the request handler, when `req.response().end()` is called the stream transitions to `closed` state, but it could still process buffers.

So we do have this conflict happening and find a way to solve it.

One way could be to delay the actual close when the response is ended, which would I believe work but introduces some complexity (i.e a special case to handle). That is most likely what we will have to do to solve this.

title: Client using HTTP/2.2 does not generate the spans of kind CLIENT when upgrading (first request)
body:
### Version

4.3.7

### Context

Using the Vert.x client and the protocol to HTTP/2, the span of kind `CLIENT` that is made by Opentelemetry is ignored in the first request. 

This is because the connection is upgraded to become an HTTP/2 connection via (this is done by [Http2UpgradeClientConnection](https://github.com/eclipse-vertx/vert.x/blob/master/src/main/java/io/vertx/core/http/impl/Http2UpgradeClientConnection.java)). 

Then, the `Http2UpgradeClientConnection` implementation will call the method [current.createStream](https://github.com/eclipse-vertx/vert.x/blob/011d271bf470600989a59a605dee05ae92034170/src/main/java/io/vertx/core/http/impl/Http2UpgradeClientConnection.java#L758) where `current` is an instance of [Http1xClientConnection](https://github.com/eclipse-vertx/vert.x/blob/master/src/main/java/io/vertx/core/http/impl/Http1xClientConnection.java) in the first request. So, a stream of type [Http1xClientConnection.StreamImpl](https://github.com/eclipse-vertx/vert.x/blob/011d271bf470600989a59a605dee05ae92034170/src/main/java/io/vertx/core/http/impl/Http1xClientConnection.java#L413) is created and all the CLIENT traces will be added in this stream (see [here](https://github.com/eclipse-vertx/vert.x/blob/011d271bf470600989a59a605dee05ae92034170/src/main/java/io/vertx/core/http/impl/Http1xClientConnection.java#L276)). 

And the problem is that when ending the first request (and producing the traces), the connection has been already upgraded, so it's using one of type `Http2ClientConnection` which uses a new of type [Http2ClientConnection.StreamImpl](https://github.com/eclipse-vertx/vert.x/blob/011d271bf470600989a59a605dee05ae92034170/src/main/java/io/vertx/core/http/impl/Http2ClientConnection.java#L390) which does not have the CLIENT traces that was created in Http1xClientConnection.StreamImpl.

At the second request, the connection has been already upgraded, so the `current` variable in Http2UpgradeClientConnection is a `Http2ClientConnection` instance, so everything works as expected.

title: Disable writeHandler registration for net sockets and websockets by default
body:
When a net socket is created, it registers a local consumer which address is given by `io.vertx.core.net.NetSocket#writeHandlerID`.

Similarly, when a websocket is created, it registers local consumers which addresses are given by `io.vertx.core.http.WebSocketBase#binaryHandlerID` and `io.vertx.core.http.WebSocketBase#textHandlerID`.

This puts some pressure on cluster managers when Vert.x is clustered, even if most users don't need the feature.

We shall disable write handlers registration by default (as we did for SockJS handler in https://github.com/vert-x3/vertx-web/issues/1221).

This is a breaking (behavioral) change, but users will be able to switch the feature on with options.

body:
### Questions

Allow semicolon to be treated as normal character in query params

### Version

4.3.7

### Context

1. Client sends a request to an API e.g. http://host/someBasePath/myResource?transactionDetails=shopping;tesco&date=2013-01-01
2. Notice the `;` within 'shopping;tesco'
3. The API internally tries to fetch the query params from the `HttpServerRequest` i.e
   `httpServerRequest.getParam("transactionDetails")`
   Expectation is this would return `shopping;tesco` however it is only returning `shopping` instead

Semicolons since 2014 from W3C recommendations are now illegal parameter separators and only `&` is allowed.
There is a fix merged in netty -> https://github.com/netty/netty/issues/8855 (see QueryStringDecoder class)

However HttpServerRequest doesn't seem to allow a way to get query params with treating semicolons as normal.

It appears this is down to HttpUtils using a constructor of QueryStringDecoder which default to not treating semicolons as normal characters:
https://github.com/eclipse-vertx/vert.x/blob/1807f72a01c70bb9c189ee232ce635d15be0d726/src/main/java/io/vertx/core/http/impl/HttpUtils.java#L498

Should the above HttpUtils now use the new constructor of QueryStringDecoder and set semicolons to be treated as normal characters by default from vertx point of view? Alternatively some way for users of vertx to set this behaviour on/off?

* Vertx 4.3.7

title: Future terminal operations clarification
body:
In some parts of the stack, it is assumed that `Future` terminal operations (`onSuccess`, `onFailure`, `onComplete`) are executed in order of registration.

While in most cases this is true, it is not guaranteed and can lead to bugs like https://github.com/vert-x3/vertx-jdbc-client/issues/281

The actual behavior should be clarified in documentation and we should inspect the stack to find possible problems.

title: Let users define a codec to use when no codec was found
body:
- Register codecs as usual
- Provide a function to the `EventBus`; the function is invoked when no codec has been found for message body and must return a user codec name

This can solve a few use cases, for example:

- selecting a codec that does nothing for objects to deliver locally if the user knows the object is immutable
- user has many objects generated from `.proto` files and wants to defer to [Protocol Buffers](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers) for serialization / deserialization
- user wants to use JSON codec for any object

Sample usage:

```java
EncodeEveryThingWithJacksonCodec everyThingWithJacksonCodec = new EncodeEveryThingWithJacksonCodec();
vertx.eventBus().registerCodec(everyThingWithJacksonCodec);
vertx.eventBus().codecSelector(body -> everyThingWithJacksonCodec.name());
```

### Version

VertX 4.2.6

### Context

[ClusterEventBus uses NetServer#listen](https://github.com/eclipse-vertx/vert.x/blob/master/src/main/java/io/vertx/core/eventbus/impl/clustered/ClusteredEventBus.java#L90) internally but this adds a

1. Clustered VertX instance Producer constantly send / publish "foo" to "address"
2. Clustered VertX instance Consumer consuming "address"
3. Having a **shutdown delay** in the consumer - delay for 5 seconds (we use this "trick" to remove our microservices from discovery - finish processing - then really closing vertx)
4. close Consumer instance

title: ArrayList concurrency error when deploying the verticles
Support vfs protocol in the default FileResolver implementation
body:
#### Read me

When an embedded Vertx is used for a war deployment which reads resources in the bundle, and it is deployed to a WildFly server, it fails to read with error message: `Invalid url protocol: vfs`.

It is more like a feature than a bug from Vert.x point of view.

For more information, please refer to https://github.com/gaol/tests/tree/master/vertx/vfs-resolver for the reproducer.

#### Describe the feature

The default FileResolver implementation [supports several URL protocols](https://github.com/eclipse-vertx/vert.x/blob/4.2.3/src/main/java/io/vertx/core/file/impl/FileResolverImpl.java#L235-L239) to resolve the file path, I would like to add the support of `vfs`.

`vfs` comes from [jboss-vfs](https://github.com/jbossas/jboss-vfs) project, which is used inside of WildFly server for managing the files of the deployed applications, any resource loaded by the class loader(ModuleClassLoader) is a vfs URL in the server.

Using a customized FileResolver implementation looks too much than just one line modification in the default implementation, so it is great to have it supported in Vert.x.

#### Use cases

When embedded Vertx is used in web application, and it is deployed to WildFly server, it faces this problem.
Like when [PropertyFileAuthentication](https://vertx.io/docs/vertx-auth-properties/java/) is used to read authentication properties from the bundle.

title: Have a dedicated exception on timed out connections
body:
#### Description

Using the Vert.x HTTP client, when a connection takes too long and reaches its time out, we get this exception : 
```
io.vertx.core.VertxException: Connection was closed
```

This does not help in understanding the connection timeout has been reached.

So I would prefer to have either : 
- a dedicated Exception carrying this information (so we can react accordingly)
- an explicit error message to be able to investigate easily

#### Use cases

- Easier bug investigation
- Ability to react to timed out connection accordingly

#### Contribution

I've investigated a bit and found out the issue was at the interface of Netty and Vertx : `io.vertx.core.net.impl.ConnectionBase`. On Idle connection event, Vert.x simply closes the connection.

title: Provide a way to access the vert.x file cache directory
body:
Vert.x uses a file cache to hold resources from the class path. This allows vert.x to get better performance on file IO and users to safely pack resources with their applications.

Given that such cache is per vert.x instance, we cannot rely on system properties to know where is the location of the instance cache. For this, users have been using a non specified behavior `VertxInternal#resolveFile("")` to compute the location.

This has several problems:

1. It is not guaranteed to work when cache is disabled
2. It doesn't respect the `vertx.cwd` variable
3. it is expensive as it may go over the classpath file resolution

For this we should add an internal API to return the path or `null` if cache is disabled.

title: Promises/futures with context do not always use context exception handler
body:
### Version

4.1.2

### Description

If a promise is completed or failed, any handler attached to the associated future may throw an exception. How that exception is handled currently depends on several factors:

1. Future has a context, but the future is completed/failed on a different context:
    * Behavior: The exception is given to context.reportException() and does not bubble up.
2. Future has a context, and the future is completed/failed on that context:
    * Behavior: The exception bubbles up to whatever completed/failed the promise.
3. Future does not have a context:
    * Behavior: The exception bubbles up to whatever completed/failed the promise.

The behavior of situation 2 should match 1. But it currently matches 3. This behavior is due to the if() statement at https://github.com/eclipse-vertx/vert.x/blob/4.1.2/src/main/java/io/vertx/core/impl/future/FutureBase.java#L50.

See #1568 for the discussion that led to the creation of this issue.

title: PKCS12 Keystore format when running in a FIPS-restricted JRE
body:
### Version

3.9.8, but later versions appear to have the same issue.

### Context

We are developing a number of applications that need to be able to run in a JRE that has all non-FIPS compliant encryption formats disabled/removed. We have a `BCFKS` KeyStore, and we are able to read it in, however, we get an error because Vert.x then tries to initialize an internal `PKCS12` KeyStore, which is not present in our environment:
```
io.vertx.core.VertxException: java.security.KeyStoreException: PKCS12 not found
```
We traced the issue to the `createEmptyKeyStore` function in `/src/main/java/io/vertx/core/net/impl/KeyStoreHelper.java`, which hard-codes the new empty keystore to the `PKCS12` format. We verified that we could create a custom build of Vert.x with the hard-coded value changed to `BCFKS`, and Vert.x then successfully runs on the affected environment, however this is not a practical long-term solution. 

### Do you have a reproducer?

To reproduce, you will need to remove the `PKCS12` KeyStore format from the JRE's `lib/security/java.security` file. To do this, find the list of providers and comment out the line containing `com.sun.net.ssl.internal.ssl.Provider`. Save the file, and then read in a (non-PKCS12) KeyStore using Vert.x.

```

keystore.type=BCFKS
```

Will then mean that using the method referred in the previous comment will return `BCFKS` as expected.

`KeyStore.getDefaultType()` works for our use case (our default is already set to `BCFKS`). The only downside is, as @pmlopes mentioned, that it will cause Java 8 to regress to using `JKS` rather than `PKCS12`.
@pmlopes as @kjrokos said we should fallback instead of using the default type which is not intended on Java 8

IMO, defaulting to `PKCS12` and falling back to `getDefaultType()` has the somewhat strange property that you can change the keystore format to e.g., be FIPS compliant, but only if you disable the `PKCS12` format. This is the case for us, but I'm not sure if it's the case in general. I'd prefer using `getDefaultType()` as the primary, but upgrade to `PKCS12` if `getDefaultType()` returns `jks` (and `PKCS12` exists).

Another alternative would be to use the type specified in `io.vertx.core.net.KeyStoreOptions`. The advantage being that no modification of the `java.security` file is necessary, and we could continue to use `PKCS12` as the default unless the user explicitly overrides it. I'm not sure how feasible that is, however - at first glance it looks like it would require touching a lot of code.

FWIW, I'm happy to make a PR for whichever solution is agreed upon if you'd like.
